    Building a benchmark group?

    No single group serves every purpose. Compensation, enrollment, finance, and strategic planning call for different comparison groups, and boards, faculty, and regulators evaluate each in context. We help institutions engage in a thoughtful, systematic, and reproducible discernment process that results in comparison groups designed for their purpose and able to withstand scrutiny.

      Natural groups and benchmarks

      Conferences, systems, and shared traditions, which we call natural groups, rank among the most common reasons institutions select one another. Although these natural groups offer a convenient starting point for a comparison, their members often vary widely in resources, size, student body, academic portfolio, and other important characteristics. A proper comparison group must take the relevant characteristics into consideration to suit its specific purpose.

      Membership as reported to IPEDS for each collection. Conferences: NCAA and NAIA conferences in any of football, basketball, baseball, or cross country and track. Athletic associations: national memberships such as the NCAA and NAIA. See the Glossary.

      Building a benchmark group?

      Natural groups offer a reasonable first approximation. Developing a comparison group suited to a particular purpose requires a thoughtful, systematic, and reproducible approach.

          About the data

          Each year, colleges and universities may name for the federal government the institutions that should serve as their comparisons. IPEDS publishes these selections, and together they map how American higher education sees itself.

          Why comparison groups matter

          Most institutional measures gain meaning only beside the same measures at other institutions. Does a tuition discount run high? Do faculty salaries compete in the market? Does an endowment look large for an institution of its type? Boards, presidents, cabinets, and faculty ask such questions routinely, and the answers depend on the comparison. Twenty well-endowed research universities and twenty regional teaching institutions will portray the same institution in very different terms. The choice of comparison group is perhaps the most important step in shaping a benchmarking study.

          Where the data come from

          The Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) consists of annual surveys administered by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES), part of the U.S. Department of Education. Federal law requires every institution that participates in, or applies to participate in, the federal student aid programs authorized by Title IV of the Higher Education Act to complete them; other institutions may report voluntarily. The surveys cover admissions, enrollment, degrees awarded, graduation rates, finances, staffing, salaries, and student financial aid, and NCES makes the results public. IPEDS organizes its data by collection, labeled by academic year (for example, 2024-25). The Glossary defines these and related terms.

          Two kinds of comparison groups

          Each year NCES prepares a Data Feedback Report for each reporting institution, summarizing its data alongside those of a comparison group. That group comes from one of two sources.

          • A custom comparison group the institution selects. An institution may submit a list of 1 to 100 comparison institutions. IPEDS publishes these custom comparison groups, which this site displays; people commonly call them peer groups.
          • A comparison group NCES assigns. When an institution does not submit a custom group, NCES constructs one from characteristics such as control (public or private), degree level, and Carnegie Classification.

          A custom comparison group reflects a deliberate choice, typically by an institutional research office and sometimes with senior leadership. That deliberateness gives these groups their interest: they record the institutions an institution itself considers appropriate comparisons.

          How institutions select comparison institutions

          The data do not record why an institution chose its comparisons, but the reasons generally fall into a few categories:

          • Competitors: institutions that recruit the same students or draw on the same pools of faculty and staff.
          • Comparable institutions: institutions with a similar mission, size, academic portfolio, resources, or setting.
          • Aspirational institutions: institutions an institution hopes to resemble in the future.
          • Natural groups: members of the same state system, athletic conference, religious tradition, or consortium.

          Most groups combine these categories. A group built for one purpose, such as recruitment, may poorly serve another, such as compensation. A single group is generally not appropriate for all benchmarking purposes.

          Who submits a comparison group

          Interpreting these data

          • Submission remains optional. Only institutions that submit a custom comparison group have selections of their own on this site. About two-thirds of reporting institutions do not submit one, most of them for-profit institutions or institutions whose programs last less than two years.
          • Each group serves a single report. The Data Feedback Report defines its official purpose. Some institutions select close competitors, others aspirational institutions, and others a state system or consortium; the data do not distinguish among these motives.
          • Most selections go unreturned. Only about one selection in six runs both ways. A selection reflects how the selecting institution views the selected one, not the reverse.
          • Frequency of selection does not rank institutions. An institution may draw many selections because it serves as a familiar reference point, an aspiration, or one of many similar institutions in its region.
          • Groups change slowly. Most groups remain identical from one year to the next, so a group may reflect how an institution viewed its comparisons several years earlier. The collection boxes on the Explore page show when each group last changed.
          • This site counts only groups submitted in a given year. IPEDS publishes custom comparison groups in one table and, separately, a flag indicating whether each institution submitted a group. Through 2023-24 the two agree. The 2024-25 release, however, includes groups for about 770 institutions that, according to the IPEDS flag, did not submit one, some of which closed years earlier; these appear to represent previously saved groups. Including them would add roughly 15,000 selections and alter which institutions appear most often selected, so we exclude them.
          • Names and figures reflect the latest data. Each institution appears with its most recent IPEDS name and values (enrollment, finances, Carnegie Classification), not as it appeared when selected. A small number of selected institutions have since closed or merged.
          • Size and wealth tell only part of the story. The comparisons on the Explore page use four measures: expenses, endowment, total FTE, and the six-year graduation rate. A sound comparison group also weighs mission, academic programs, student characteristics, region, and the purpose of the comparison.

          How we use these data

          In our work, an institution's own custom comparison group and the institutions that select it offer two perspectives among several. We consider them alongside the group NCES assigns and groups built from explicit criteria suited to the question, so leaders can see whether a conclusion holds across groups or depends on a particular choice.

          Does your comparison group still fit?

          Much in higher education has changed over the past five to ten years, and a comparison group can drift away from the purpose it once served. We welcome a conversation about your institution's groups: what each conveys, how well each suits its purpose today, and whether the time has come for a fresh look.

          Which measures matter for your question?

          A single year of IPEDS contains approximately 2,450 variables, and sources such as the College Scorecard, the Carnegie Classifications, and compensation surveys add many more. Selecting the right measures begins with clarifying the decisions the comparison group will inform. From there, we help institutions work through a thoughtful, systematic, and reproducible process to discern the groups that best serve those decisions.

          Work with us

          The Casagrande Institute helps colleges, universities, and higher education associations align compensation practices with mission, market, and means. We conduct executive, faculty, and staff compensation studies, including building and reviewing the comparison groups behind each analysis, and serve as external evaluators for grant-funded programs.

          What we do

          Executive compensation

          We analyze compensation for presidents and senior leaders against carefully constructed comparison groups, drawing on public Form 990 filings and national survey data, in the form governing boards require for their review.

          Faculty compensation

          We examine salary structures and ranges, disciplinary differentials, equity and compression, and the projected cost of adopting a new structure.

          Staff compensation

          We compare staff positions with the relevant markets, both within and beyond higher education, and analyze the regional cost of labor.

          Grant evaluation

          We serve as external evaluators for federal and foundation grants, from the evaluation plan in the proposal through data collection and annual and summative reports.

          Why comparison groups matter to our work

          Every compensation study rests on a comparison. A board judges a president's pay against presidents of similar institutions, a faculty salary structure draws its ranges from comparable colleges and universities, and staff pay follows the labor markets that compete for the same people. The comparison group defines the market and shapes the conclusions, so we construct it with care.

          Grant evaluation seldom calls for a comparison group, yet it rests on the same habits: a clear purpose, explicit criteria, careful attention to detail, and a systematic and reproducible process. Whatever the engagement, we approach our work with collaboration, care, and integrity.
